video_title: Why Treasuries Are ‘Risky’ Again | Odd Lots
gist: Chicago Harris economist Carolin Pflueger argues the surge in long Treasury yields (30-year at 5.59%, highest since 2002) mainly reflects Treasuries becoming riskier, more stock-like assets, and that the Fed's perceived reaction function is learned from actions. She also links bond markets to geopolitical hegemony.

insights.claim: Treasuries were not always safe: in the 1970s-90s they were viewed as risky, with positive bond-stock correlation. After 2000 the correlation turned negative (bonds hedged equities), and in the most recent period bond risk has risen again.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Bond-equity diversification is regime-dependent; a 60/40 hedge cannot be assumed.

insights.claim: A positive bond-stock correlation means there is nowhere to hide in a stock-bond portfolio, which is part of why 2022 was so painful.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Portfolio hedging breaks down exactly when yields rise and equities fall together.

insights.claim: Pre-2000 bond risk was largely inflation-driven (UK inflation-linked data show a big chunk on the inflation side). Post-2000 the inflation component shrank and both nominal and real bond risks were negative. The recent rise has been less inflation-based and more in index-linked bonds, and is not yet back to 1980s levels.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Recent bond risk is not a pure replay of the 1980s inflation regime.

insights.claim: The shift around 2000 is explained by shock type: in the 1980s stagflation (supply shocks) hurt nominal bonds and stocks together, whereas postwar demand-type recessions were low-inflation, so nominal bonds benefited.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Supply-shock regimes (oil, fiscal credibility) make bonds stock-like; demand-shock regimes make them hedges.

insights.claim: A return to 1980s-style risky bond markets requires a perfect storm: inflationary supply shocks (oil, fiscal credibility loss, moving inflation expectations) plus a Fed willing or forced to accept a recession.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: The tail risk is conditional on Fed behaviour, not just on shocks.

themes.theme: Why long yields are rising: risk pricing

insights.claim: The 30-year Treasury yield was about 5.59% at recording (Sept 29), the highest since 2002, and kept climbing even after a Fed rate hike following Jackson Hole.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal / Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: A hike failing to cap long yields raises doubts about transmission to financial conditions.

insights.claim: Bonds becoming riskier (more stock-like) should raise required returns. Expected returns priced in bonds, measured using forecast-based yields to strip out forecast error, track bond-stock comovement closely across maturities and developed markets.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Higher yields reflect compensation for risk, not just inflation or supply.

insights.claim: Back-of-envelope: roughly a quarter of the decline in the 10-year yield from the mid-1980s to the 2010s came from Treasuries becoming better hedges, with the rest largely lower inflation expectations. Most of the 2020-2025 rise in the 10-year yield can be explained by bonds becoming more stock-like.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Hedge-quality, not inflation expectations, is the main driver of the recent selloff.

insights.claim: Long-term inflation expectations have been quite stable over the past 5-7 years despite high realized inflation, so rising yields reflect risk compensation. However, nominal and real yields have delinked since 2000, indicating more inflation uncertainty even with stable averages.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Watch inflation-risk premia and nominal-real delinking rather than breakevens alone.

insights.claim: The change in the safety of Treasuries themselves is a substantial component of the long-run yield story, alongside the natural rate and safe-asset demand, though not exclusive of them.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Structural-yield debates should include bond riskiness.

insights.claim: On supply, Ricardian equivalence is a useful first approximation: taxpayers hold the bonds, so debt supply moves money from one pocket to another. Her results suggest bond risk is priced mainly against stock-market exposure, though bond-specific holder exposure probably matters too. She concedes reality violates it.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Deficit-driven supply is not the whole yield story; equity-linked risk is a priced channel.

insights.claim: The perceived policy reaction function (what markets expect the Fed to do in response to inflation and output) can be measured two ways: Blue Chip forecaster regressions of forecast fed funds on forecast inflation and output gap, and yield responses to macro announcement surprises. The two give similar answers.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Gives a way to evaluate Fed communication and framework changes.

insights.claim: A well-understood reaction function lets markets do the Fed's work: yields adjust to data before the next FOMC meeting, speeding transmission.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: If the reaction function is misread, tightening may not pass through to yields.

insights.claim: In 2021 the perceived reaction function was nearly flat: with rates at zero and average inflation targeting, forecasters, whether high- or low-inflation, expected zero rates. After a May 2021 inflation surprise of about half a percent (roughly 6% annualized), the 2-year yield did not move.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: The Fed's 2021 stance left inflation unanchored in rate expectations, a lesson for communication.

insights.claim: The perceived inflation response went from about 0 to about 1 only between early 2022 and late 2023, after the Fed started hiking. Markets learn from actions rather than words.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Credibility for a new regime is built by acting, which means painful early moves.

insights.claim: The perceived reaction to output is steeper in tightening cycles (data-dependent) and flatter in easings, which tend to be sudden with little else expected.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Data matters more for rate expectations when the Fed is tightening.

insights.claim: A more gradual, inertial monetary policy rule gained credibility post-2000 and can keep bonds bond-like, since a soft landing priced in means stocks need not fall when yields rise. Central bank credibility is the background condition for this.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Credibility loss would push bonds back toward being risky.

insights.claim: In estimating the reaction function, adding a triple-A spread forecast as a financial conditions proxy gave only a small coefficient and did not change the macro responses, offering limited evidence that financial-conditions targeting shifts it. She declined to speak for Kevin Warsh.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Fed reflexivity via financial conditions looks second-order in her data.

insights.claim: Bond markets historically are tied to winning wars: Hamilton in 1790 called US credit the price of liberty, and the UK's deep bond market and low rates before the Napoleonic Wars helped it win and become the dominant financial power. The US held a similar position in the second half of the 20th century.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Military and financial advantages reinforce each other.

insights.claim: In a Pflueger-Read model, with tiny bond markets the natural-moat country is safest; with moderate borrowing capacity there is a tipping point; with very high borrowing capacity and debt/GDP, expectations become self-fulfilling and a hegemonic transition could occur through financial markets alone, without war. She calls the last case hypothetical.
insights.speaker: Carolin Pflueger
insights.so_what: Cheap-financing expectations could shift hegemony without a war.

insights.claim: Chinese 30-year government bond yields were about 2% against 5.6% for the US 30-year. Weisenthal added that the generic Chinese vs US 10-year spread flipped during Covid, with US yields rising to a 300-350 bp premium, and the Chinese downtrend began around 2018-19 when China was added to indices.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway / Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: A relative-funding-cost gap favors China's financing of industry and military; index inclusion was a catalyst.

insights.claim: Compounding logic: cheaper borrowing funds productivity and military investment, which snowballs over decades. The US reindustrialization push (ships, robotics) will cost more at today's rates than 10-15 years ago.
insights.speaker: Joe Weisenthal
insights.so_what: Higher rates raise the cost of defense-industrial rebuilding.

insights.claim: Backdrop named by hosts: a volatile tariff schedule, a war in Iran with spending and oil shocks, and doubts about US military strength, all feeding questions about dollar hegemony. Pflueger said geopolitics sits at a broader horizon than her usual research.
insights.speaker: Tracy Alloway
insights.so_what: Policy volatility is a plausible contributor to Treasury risk premia.
